learning.javascript:
A singly linked list is a linear data structure made up of nodes, where each node stores a value (.value) and a pointer (.next) to the following node. The last node's .next pointer is null, marking the end of the list.

Reading the picture: the list is known by its head, its first node. Each node holds a value (here, a word) and next, which leads to the following node. To reach "World!", start at the head and follow next once. The last node's next is null: there's nothing after it.

It's called singly linked because each node knows only the node after it. (A doubly linked list also gives each node a link back to the one before.)

In JavaScript, .next holds a reference to another node object: setting a.next = b doesn't copy b, it makes a point at it.

Making and linking nodes

Make nodes with the constructor. One argument makes a list of one node; give it a second argument, another node, and that node comes next:

const oneNode = new SinglyLinkedListNode("Hello");
const twoNodes = new SinglyLinkedListNode("Hello", new SinglyLinkedListNode("World!"));
// and so on ...

oneNode is a one-node list: "Hello", whose next is null. twoNodes is the two-node list in the picture. Read the nested call from the inside out: the inner call makes the "World!" node first, and the outer call makes the "Hello" node with that as its next. Each variable holds the list's head.

References

  • Gayle Laakmann McDowell, Cracking the Coding Interview, 6th edition (Palo Alto, CA: CareerCup, 2015), ISBN 978-0-9847828-5-7. Chapter 2, Linked Lists:
    • p. 92: singly and doubly linked lists, why reaching the k-th item is slow but adding at the front is fast, and building a list from a node class, including appending by walking to the end.
    • p. 93: deleting a node, the “runner” (two-pointer) technique, and recursive approaches.
    • pp. 94–95: interview questions 2.1 to 2.8.
    • pp. 207–226: solutions to those questions.
    The book's examples are in Java, and its node calls the stored value data where this question uses value.

A singly linked list is a linear data structure made up of nodes, where each node stores a value (.value) and a pointer (.next) to the following node. The last node's .next pointer is nullptr, marking the end of the list.

Reading the picture: the list is known by its head, its first node. Each node holds a value (here, a word) and next, which leads to the following node. To reach "World!", start at the head and follow next once. The last node's next is nullptr: there's nothing after it.

It's called singly linked because each node knows only the node after it. (A doubly linked list also gives each node a link back to the one before.)

In C++, next really is a pointer: its type is SinglyLinkedListNode*, the memory address of the following node. When you have a pointer to a node, reach its fields with -> rather than .: head->value, head->next. (a->b is shorthand for (*a).b.)

description.javascript:
A singly linked list is a linear data structure made up of nodes, where each node stores a value (.value) and a pointer (.next) to the following node. The last node's .next pointer is null, marking the end of the list.

You are given the SinglyLinkedListNode class below, which takes a .value and an optional .next pointer. Using only this class, construct a singly linked list where each node holds one word from the phrase "Hello World!", in order, and return the head of the list.
